claim: Obesity is causing 3.4 million deaths worldwide.
source: Data by the Global Burden of Disease Study estimate that overweight and obesity are causing 3.4 million deaths and 3.8% of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) worldwide (Lim et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Global Burden of Disease Study (Lim et al., 2012).

claim: Obesity is causing 3.8% of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) worldwide.
source: Data by the Global Burden of Disease Study estimate that overweight and obesity are causing 3.4 million deaths and 3.8% of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) worldwide (Lim et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Global Burden of Disease Study (Lim et al., 2012).

claim: Obesity promotes diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.
source: Moreover, obesity is promoting numerous disorders including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer (Saltiel and Kahn, 2001; Khandekar et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saltiel and Kahn, 2001 and Khandekar et al., 2011.

claim: Therapeutic approaches including diets or approved pharmacological interventions treating obesity have only had limited success.
source: Therapeutic approaches including diets or approved pharmacological interventions treating obesity and related co-morbidities have only had limited success (Yanovski and Yanovski, 2014; Gloy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yanovski and Yanovski, 2014 and Gloy et al., 2013.

claim: Bariatric surgery including sleeve gastrectomies has been successful in achieving sustained body weight loss.
source: Bariatric surgery including sleeve gastrectomies (SGx) has been successful in achieving a sustained body weight loss (Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2014.

claim: Bariatric surgery is an effective treatment of obesity-associated type 2 diabetes.
source: Moreover, these procedures also display an effective treatment of obesity-associated type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Schauer et al., 2014) with durable HbA1C remissions (Arterburn et al., 2013), improved insulin sensitivity, and glycemic control (Buchwald et al., 2004), all resulting into long-term reduction of overall mortality and obesity- related risk factors (Gloy et al., 2013; Sjöström, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schauer et al., 2014, Arterburn et al., 2013, Buchwald et al., 2004, Gloy et al., 2013, and Sjöström, 2013.

claim: Bariatric surgery leads to durable HbA1C remissions.
source: Moreover, these procedures also display an effective treatment of obesity-associated type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Schauer et al., 2014) with durable HbA1C remissions (Arterburn et al., 2013), improved insulin sensitivity, and glycemic control (Buchwald et al., 2004), all resulting into long-term reduction of overall mortality and obesity- related risk factors (Gloy et al., 2013; Sjöström, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Arterburn et al., 2013.

claim: Bariatric surgery improves insulin sensitivity and glycemic control.
source: Moreover, these procedures also display an effective treatment of obesity-associated type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Schauer et al., 2014) with durable HbA1C remissions (Arterburn et al., 2013), improved insulin sensitivity, and glycemic control (Buchwald et al., 2004), all resulting into long-term reduction of overall mortality and obesity- related risk factors (Gloy et al., 2013; Sjöström, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buchwald et al., 2004.

claim: Bariatric surgery results in long-term reduction of overall mortality and obesity-related risk factors.
source: Moreover, these procedures also display an effective treatment of obesity-associated type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Schauer et al., 2014) with durable HbA1C remissions (Arterburn et al., 2013), improved insulin sensitivity, and glycemic control (Buchwald et al., 2004), all resulting into long-term reduction of overall mortality and obesity- related risk factors (Gloy et al., 2013; Sjöström, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gloy et al., 2013 and Sjöström, 2013.

claim: SGx has been conceptualized to elicit weight loss by physically restricting gastric capacity.
source: SGx has been conceptualized to elicit weight loss by physically restricting gastric capacity (Gumbs et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gumbs et al., 2007.

claim: SGx leads to a weight-independent reduction in plasma triglyceride levels.
source: Moreover, the procedure leads to a weight-independent reduction in plasma triglyceride levels (Stefater et al., 2011), improved HDL levels (Benaiges et al., 2011), increased hepatic insulin sensitivity (Chambers et al., 2011), and weight-independent alterations of gut-derived anti-diabetic hormones (GLP-1 and PYY; Peterli et al., 2009), implicating an altered metabolic profile.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stefater et al., 2011.

claim: SGx leads to improved HDL levels.
source: Moreover, the procedure leads to a weight-independent reduction in plasma triglyceride levels (Stefater et al., 2011), improved HDL levels (Benaiges et al., 2011), increased hepatic insulin sensitivity (Chambers et al., 2011), and weight-independent alterations of gut-derived anti-diabetic hormones (GLP-1 and PYY; Peterli et al., 2009), implicating an altered metabolic profile.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Benaiges et al., 2011.

claim: SGx leads to increased hepatic insulin sensitivity.
source: Moreover, the procedure leads to a weight-independent reduction in plasma triglyceride levels (Stefater et al., 2011), improved HDL levels (Benaiges et al., 2011), increased hepatic insulin sensitivity (Chambers et al., 2011), and weight-independent alterations of gut-derived anti-diabetic hormones (GLP-1 and PYY; Peterli et al., 2009), implicating an altered metabolic profile.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chambers et al., 2011.

claim: SGx leads to weight-independent alterations of gut-derived anti-diabetic hormones (GLP-1 and PYY).
source: Moreover, the procedure leads to a weight-independent reduction in plasma triglyceride levels (Stefater et al., 2011), improved HDL levels (Benaiges et al., 2011), increased hepatic insulin sensitivity (Chambers et al., 2011), and weight-independent alterations of gut-derived anti-diabetic hormones (GLP-1 and PYY; Peterli et al., 2009), implicating an altered metabolic profile.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peterli et al., 2009.

claim: Bile acids activate nuclear transcription factors involved in hepatic glucose metabolism.
source: Bile acids have been shown to activate nuclear transcription factors involved in hepatic glucose metabolism (Parks et al., 1999) that promote GLP-1 secretion via signaling by the bile acid receptor TGR5 (Thomas et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parks et al., 1999.

claim: Bile acids promote GLP-1 secretion via signaling by the bile acid receptor TGR5.
source: Bile acids have been shown to activate nuclear transcription factors involved in hepatic glucose metabolism (Parks et al., 1999) that promote GLP-1 secretion via signaling by the bile acid receptor TGR5 (Thomas et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2009.

claim: Bile acids are essential for SGx-derived weight loss through signaling via the bile acid receptor FXR.
source: Moreover, bile acids have been identified to be essential for SGx-derived weight loss through signaling via the bile acid receptor FXR (Ryan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ryan et al., 2014.

claim: Various studies have reported increasing serum bile acids following SGx in experimental and clinical studies.
source: Consistently, various studies have reported increasing serum bile acids following SGx in experimental and clinical studies (Myronovych et al., 2014; Albaugh et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Myronovych et al., 2014 and Albaugh et al., 2015.

claim: C57BL/6 DIO mice underwent SGx and showed significant weight loss (-34% by 2 weeks).
source: Subsequent to SGx, we observed a significant weight loss (−34% by 2 weeks).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sham-operated DIO mice re-gained their pre-operative weight by post-operative day 14 (-5%).
source: In marked contrast, sham-operated DIO mice re-gained their pre-operative weight by post-operative day 14 (−5%), indicating that the observed weight loss was independent of the surgical trauma (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1B.

claim: SGx-induced weight loss is independent of the surgical trauma.
source: In marked contrast, sham-operated DIO mice re-gained their pre-operative weight by post-operative day 14 (−5%), indicating that the observed weight loss was independent of the surgical trauma (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison between SGx and sham-operated mice.

claim: SGx promotes durable weight loss independent of the surgical procedure or dietary effects.
source: Thus, SGx promoted durable weight loss independent of the surgical procedure or dietary effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results comparing SGx and sham-operated mice.

claim: SGx induces modifications in levels of metabolic and intestinal hormones.
source: Previous studies implicated that SGx induce modifications in levels of metabolic and intestinal hormones (Stefater et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stefater et al., 2012.

claim: Quantitative metabolomic profiling detected 260 metabolites with 17 candidates showing significant statistical difference between lean and DIO mice.
source: Our unbiased approach detected 260 metabolites with 17 candidates showing a significant statistical difference between lean and DIO mice by analysis of variance (ANOVA), heat mapping, and SAM (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2A,B.

claim: DIO mice have significantly decreased systemic levels of TDCA and L-valine.
source: We found significantly decreased systemic levels of TDCA and L-valine in DIO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from metabolomic profiling.

claim: Obese animals that underwent SGx displayed overall restored levels of TDCA and valine.
source: Obese animals, that underwent SGx, however, displayed overall restored levels of both metabolites, suggesting a critical involvement of TDCA/valine in the metabolic underpinning of SGx-induced weight loss (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2C.

claim: TDCA and valine are critically involved in the metabolic underpinning of SGx-induced weight loss.
source: Obese animals, that underwent SGx, however, displayed overall restored levels of both metabolites, suggesting a critical involvement of TDCA/valine in the metabolic underpinning of SGx-induced weight loss (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TDCA and valine levels are restored after SGx.

claim: Patients showed a significant increase in both TDCA and valine levels 3 months after SGx.
source: Subsequent to clinical SGx, we observed a significant increase in both TDCA and valine levels, indicating a similar impact of SGx in mice and humans (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from human samples presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2D.

claim: SGx has a similar impact on TDCA and valine levels in mice and humans.
source: Subsequent to clinical SGx, we observed a significant increase in both TDCA and valine levels, indicating a similar impact of SGx in mice and humans (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of mouse and human data.

claim: Combined injection of TDCA and valine increased absolute, systemic TDCA and valine concentrations in DIO mice comparable to levels measured in lean control mice.
source: Notably, the combined injection of TDCA and valine increased absolute, systemic TDCA and valine concentrations in DIO mice comparable to levels measured in lean control mice (Figure 3A), resulting in robust weight loss (Figure 3B) that went beyond the observed effects in mice undergoing SGx (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3A.

claim: Combined injection of TDCA and valine resulted in robust weight loss in DIO mice.
source: Notably, the combined injection of TDCA and valine increased absolute, systemic TDCA and valine concentrations in DIO mice comparable to levels measured in lean control mice (Figure 3A), resulting in robust weight loss (Figure 3B) that went beyond the observed effects in mice undergoing SGx (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3B.

claim: TDCA/valine-induced weight loss went beyond the observed effects in mice undergoing SGx.
source: Notably, the combined injection of TDCA and valine increased absolute, systemic TDCA and valine concentrations in DIO mice comparable to levels measured in lean control mice (Figure 3A), resulting in robust weight loss (Figure 3B) that went beyond the observed effects in mice undergoing SGx (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3C.

claim: Administration of TDCA/valine to lean control mice did not impact weight loss.
source: Importantly, administration of TDCA/valine to lean control mice did not impact weight loss (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3B.

claim: Isolated administration of either TDCA or valine was less effective than combined administration as assessed by body weight measurements over 30 days.
source: Of note, isolated administration of either TDCA or valine was found to be less effective as assessed by body weight measurements over a course of 30 days with daily, i.p. TDCA or valine injections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TDCA/valine treatment led to a significant decrease of subcutaneous and epididymal adipose tissue stores in DIO mice comparable to effects observed in DIO mice that underwent SGx.
source: To further characterize the impact of TDCA/valine, we assessed subcutaneous and epididymal adipose tissue stores and found a significant decrease of both fat stores in TDCA/valine-treated DIO mice comparable to effects observed in DIO mice that underwent SGx (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3D.

claim: TDCA/valine treatment reduced systemic leptin levels in DIO mice.
source: Indeed, our results indicated reduced systemic leptin levels in both, SGx and TDCA/valine-treated animals (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3E.

claim: SGx reduced systemic leptin levels in DIO mice.
source: Indeed, our results indicated reduced systemic leptin levels in both, SGx and TDCA/valine-treated animals (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3E.

claim: Obesity promotes insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
source: It is well established that obesity promotes insulin resistance and T2D (Saltiel and Kahn, 2001; Xu et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saltiel and Kahn, 2001 and Xu et al., 2003.

claim: DIO mice treated with TDCA/valine displayed a complete reversal of obesity-related insulin resistance comparable to lean controls.
source: DIO mice treated with TDCA/valine displayed a complete reversal of obesity-related insulin resistance comparable to lean controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from glucose tolerance testing.

claim: Beneficial metabolic effects subsequent to TDCA/valine were analogous to those observed in DIO mice following SGx.
source: Notably, beneficial metabolic effects subsequent to TDCA/valine were analogous to those observed in DIO mice following SGx (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3F.

claim: Decreased food intake is critical for long-term weight reduction subsequent to SGx.
source: Growing evidence suggests a decreased food intake as critical for the long-term weight reduction subsequent to SGx (Stefater et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stefater et al., 2012.

claim: Cumulative energy intake significantly declined in TDCA/valine-treated animals compared to PBS-treated controls.
source: While cumulative energy intake and the hourly food intake significantly declined in TDCA/valine-treated animals compared to PBS-treated controls (Figure 4A,B), hourly measured energy expenditure and the measured total activity did not change during treatment (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from indirect calorimetry presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Hourly food intake significantly declined in TDCA/valine-treated animals compared to PBS-treated controls.
source: While cumulative energy intake and the hourly food intake significantly declined in TDCA/valine-treated animals compared to PBS-treated controls (Figure 4A,B), hourly measured energy expenditure and the measured total activity did not change during treatment (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from indirect calorimetry presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Hourly measured energy expenditure did not change during TDCA/valine treatment.
source: While cumulative energy intake and the hourly food intake significantly declined in TDCA/valine-treated animals compared to PBS-treated controls (Figure 4A,B), hourly measured energy expenditure and the measured total activity did not change during treatment (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from indirect calorimetry presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Measured total activity did not change during TDCA/valine treatment.
source: While cumulative energy intake and the hourly food intake significantly declined in TDCA/valine-treated animals compared to PBS-treated controls (Figure 4A,B), hourly measured energy expenditure and the measured total activity did not change during treatment (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from indirect calorimetry presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The respiratory exchange ratio of TDCA/valine-treated obese animals significantly declined.
source: Moreover, the respiratory exchange ratio and energy balance of TDCA/valine-treated obese animals significantly declined, supporting the significance of fatty acids for energy metabolism (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from indirect calorimetry presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The energy balance of TDCA/valine-treated obese animals significantly declined.
source: Moreover, the respiratory exchange ratio and energy balance of TDCA/valine-treated obese animals significantly declined, supporting the significance of fatty acids for energy metabolism (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from indirect calorimetry presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The decline in respiratory exchange ratio and energy balance supports the significance of fatty acids for energy metabolism in TDCA/valine-treated animals.
source: Moreover, the respiratory exchange ratio and energy balance of TDCA/valine-treated obese animals significantly declined, supporting the significance of fatty acids for energy metabolism (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on respiratory exchange ratio and energy balance.

claim: Treatment with TDCA/valine specifically targeted feeding behavior while leaving locomotor activity and energy expenditure unaffected.
source: Intriguingly, our data on weight loss induced by TDCA/valine were neither linked to a typical food-seeking behavior in response to fasting nor to unspecific toxic side effects of the applied metabolites. Instead, treatment with TDCA/valine specifically targeted feeding behavior while leaving locomotor activity and energy expenditure unaffected thus generating a negative energy balance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on food intake, locomotor activity, and energy expenditure.

claim: TDCA/valine treatment generated a negative energy balance.
source: Intriguingly, our data on weight loss induced by TDCA/valine were neither linked to a typical food-seeking behavior in response to fasting nor to unspecific toxic side effects of the applied metabolites. Instead, treatment with TDCA/valine specifically targeted feeding behavior while leaving locomotor activity and energy expenditure unaffected thus generating a negative energy balance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on food intake and energy expenditure.

claim: TDCA/valine treatment substantially attenuated the increase of MCH with fasting.
source: Our analysis revealed a substantial attenuation in the increase of MCH with fasting following TDCA/valine treatment (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5A.

claim: Obese animals treated with PBS and fasted for 12 hr prior to procurement of hypothalamus tissue showed a pronounced increase in MCH levels.
source: Obese animals treated with PBS and fasted for 12 hr prior to procurement of hypothalamus tissue showed a pronounced increase in MCH levels, findings that were in line with the orexigenic effects of this neuropeptide.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis.

claim: In TDCA/valine-treated obese animals, MCH-increase was not observed.
source: In TDCA/valine-treated obese animals, however, MCH-increase was not observed, suggesting an effect of TDCA/valine on the regulation of hypothalamic MCH expression (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5A.

claim: TDCA/valine has an effect on the regulation of hypothalamic MCH expression.
source: In TDCA/valine-treated obese animals, however, MCH-increase was not observed, suggesting an effect of TDCA/valine on the regulation of hypothalamic MCH expression (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that MCH increase is absent in TDCA/valine-treated animals.

claim: MCH centrally promotes food intake.
source: Notably, MCH has been shown to centrally promote food intake, augment anabolic energy regulation (Hervieu, 2003; Pissios and Maratos-Flier, 2003; Shimada et al., 1998), and increase body weight in experimental models (Della-Zuana et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hervieu, 2003; Pissios and Maratos-Flier, 2003; and Shimada et al., 1998.

claim: MCH augments anabolic energy regulation.
source: Notably, MCH has been shown to centrally promote food intake, augment anabolic energy regulation (Hervieu, 2003; Pissios and Maratos-Flier, 2003; Shimada et al., 1998), and increase body weight in experimental models (Della-Zuana et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hervieu, 2003; Pissios and Maratos-Flier, 2003; and Shimada et al., 1998.

claim: MCH increases body weight in experimental models.
source: Notably, MCH has been shown to centrally promote food intake, augment anabolic energy regulation (Hervieu, 2003; Pissios and Maratos-Flier, 2003; Shimada et al., 1998), and increase body weight in experimental models (Della-Zuana et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Della-Zuana et al., 2002.

claim: Treatment with MCHR1-I in DIO-obese mice led to decreased food intake and subsequent weight loss.
source: Treatment with MCHR1-I in DIO-obese mice led to decreased food intake and subsequent weight loss (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5B.

claim: Simultaneous treatment with both MCHR1-I and TDCA/valine did not further reduce food intake or promote additional weight loss in DIO mice.
source: More importantly, simultaneous treatment with both MCHR1-I and TDCA/valine did not further reduce food intake or promote additional weight loss in DIO mice, suggesting that effects of TDCA/valine are, at least in part, mediated through suppression of hypothalamic levels of MCH.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the combinatorial treatment experiment.

claim: Effects of TDCA/valine are, at least in part, mediated through suppression of hypothalamic levels of MCH.
source: More importantly, simultaneous treatment with both MCHR1-I and TDCA/valine did not further reduce food intake or promote additional weight loss in DIO mice, suggesting that effects of TDCA/valine are, at least in part, mediated through suppression of hypothalamic levels of MCH.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that MCHR1-I and TDCA/valine do not have additive effects.

claim: Central administration of MCH promotes food intake in rats.
source: Central administration of MCH has been reported to promote food intake in rats (Della-Zuana et al., 2002) while peripherally administered MCH has been shown to be unable to pass the blood-brain barrier (Kastin et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Della-Zuana et al., 2002.

claim: Peripherally administered MCH is unable to pass the blood-brain barrier.
source: Central administration of MCH has been reported to promote food intake in rats (Della-Zuana et al., 2002) while peripherally administered MCH has been shown to be unable to pass the blood-brain barrier (Kastin et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kastin et al., 2000.

claim: Obese rats rapidly lost weight under TDCA/valine treatment within 2 weeks.
source: Consistent with our findings in mice, obese rats rapidly lost weight under TDCA/valine treatment within 2 weeks (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5C.

claim: TDCA/valine-induced weight loss was significantly diminished when co-administering recombinant MCH and TDCA/valine in obese rats.
source: Strikingly, this effect was significantly diminished when co-administering recombinant MCH and TDCA/valine (Figure 5C), suggesting an inhibitory effect of TDCA/valine on MCH regulation (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5C.

claim: TDCA/valine has an inhibitory effect on MCH regulation.
source: Strikingly, this effect was significantly diminished when co-administering recombinant MCH and TDCA/valine (Figure 5C), suggesting an inhibitory effect of TDCA/valine on MCH regulation (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that recombinant MCH diminishes TDCA/valine-induced weight loss.

claim: Bariatric surgery is effective in 80–90% of obese individuals.
source: Bariatric surgery is effective in 80–90% of obese individuals and leads to sustained weight loss and significant improvement of co-morbidities (Gloy et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2014; Sjöström, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gloy et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2014; and Sjöström, 2013.

claim: Bariatric surgery leads to sustained weight loss and significant improvement of co-morbidities.
source: Bariatric surgery is effective in 80–90% of obese individuals and leads to sustained weight loss and significant improvement of co-morbidities (Gloy et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2014; Sjöström, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gloy et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2014; and Sjöström, 2013.

claim: C57BL/6 wild-type DIO mice are a well-established murine model of obesity.
source: To assess mechanisms of surgically induced weight loss through SGx, we made use of C57BL/6 wild-type DIO mice, a well-established murine model of obesity (Winzell and Ahrén, 2004; Wang and Liao, 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Winzell and Ahrén, 2004 and Wang and Liao, 2012.

claim: Durable weight loss and improved glucose tolerance are mediated through bile acid-induced FXR signaling, affecting overall food intake and feeding behavior.
source: Indeed, durable weight loss and improved glucose tolerance are mediated through bile acid-induced FXR signaling, affecting overall food intake and feeding behavior (Ryan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ryan et al., 2014.

claim: Re-feeding mice that underwent SGx with an HFD revealed that these animals gained weight without reaching pre-surgery obesity.
source: Moreover, re-feeding mice that underwent SGx with an HFD revealed that these animals gained weight without reaching pre-surgery obesity, supporting a relevant role of appetite behavior in addition to a modified metabolism (Stefater et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stefater et al., 2010.

claim: Diet-restricted DIO mice restored lost body weight by exhibiting hyperphagia, fully re-gaining their body weight with the end of the diet.
source: In contrast, diet-restricted DIO mice restored lost body weight by exhibiting hyperphagia, fully re-gaining their body weight with the end of the diet (Brownlow et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brownlow et al., 1993.

claim: A decreased food intake is likely to constitute a primary impetus for the long-term weight loss observed after SGx.
source: Hence, a decreased food intake is likely to constitute a primary impetus for the long-term weight loss observed after SGx (Stefater et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stefater et al., 2012.

claim: Rats restricted to the same daily caloric intake as SGx animals exhibited comparable weight loss.
source: In support, pair-feeding studies have shown that rats restricted to the same daily caloric intake as SGx animals exhibited comparable weight loss (Stefater et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stefater et al., 2012.

claim: Durable weight loss and amelioration of obesity-associated disorders after SGx are mediated through both, molecular and central appetite-regulating effects of TDCA/valine.
source: These findings are in line with our study, suggesting that durable weight loss and amelioration of obesity-associated disorders after SGx are mediated through both, molecular and central appetite-regulating effects of TDCA/valine.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing TDCA/valine effects on food intake and MCH.

claim: TDCA/valine-treated animals had a markedly reduced food intake without altered energy expenditure or locomotor activity.
source: Indeed, our results indicated that TDCA/valine-treated animals had a markedly reduced food intake without altered energy expenditure or locomotor activity, thus excluding toxic side effects of TDCA/valine as a potential confounder of appetite reduction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from indirect calorimetry.

claim: TDCA/valine administered to lean animals did not lead to weight loss.
source: Notably, TDCA/valine administered to lean animals did not lead to weight loss, emphasizing on appetite-regulating effects only in obese animals while excluding inflammatory processes as confounding side effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: TDCA/valine has appetite-regulating effects only in obese animals.
source: Notably, TDCA/valine administered to lean animals did not lead to weight loss, emphasizing on appetite-regulating effects only in obese animals while excluding inflammatory processes as confounding side effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TDCA/valine does not affect lean animals.

claim: Decreased food intake is a cardinal feature of SGx-induced weight loss.
source: Therefore, our observation that TDCA/valine treatment mimicked metabolic changes that result from SGx are supported by our finding that decreased food intake is a cardinal feature of SGx-induced weight loss.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results comparing TDCA/valine treatment and SGx.

claim: Increased levels of branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) have been associated with T2D and obesity-derived complications.
source: Within the last decades increased levels of branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) levels have been associated with T2D and obesity-derived complications (Lynch and Adams, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lynch and Adams, 2014.

claim: Increased BCAA levels are a consequence of obesity rather than its cause.
source: Notably, various studies have suggested increased BCAA levels to be a consequence of obesity rather than its cause.
evidence: The claim is based on a general statement about various studies.

claim: Mitochondrial impairment and obesity-derived low-grade inflammation have been associated with decreased levels of enzymes that degrade BCAA.
source: Indeed, mitochondrial impairment and obesity-derived low-grade inflammation has been associated with decreased levels of enzymes that degrade BCAA (She et al., 2007; Burrill et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to She et al., 2007 and Burrill et al., 2015.

claim: A combination of thiazolidinediones and metformin failed to demonstrate decreasing systemic BCAA levels despite an increased insulin sensitivity.
source: Moreover, a recent study employing a combination of thiazolidinediones and metformin failed to demonstrate decreasing systemic BCAA levels despite an increased insulin sensitivity (Irving et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Irving et al., 2015.

claim: The weight reducing effect of L-valine in combination with TDCA is not impacting obesity directly but rather exerts effects through a reduction of appetite.
source: We thus speculate that the weight reducing effect of L-valine in combination with TDCA is not impacting obesity directly but rather exerts effects through a reduction of appetite.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the experimental results and literature context.

claim: Supplementation of leucine to drinking water of DIO mice reduced body weight by 32% over 10 weeks.
source: Supplementation of leucine to drinking water of DIO mice reduced body weight by 32% over 10 weeks (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2007.

claim: Leucine administration induces a partial resistance to diet-induced obesity that resulted into reduced hyperglycemia and hypercholesterolemia in DIO mice.
